opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really hard question, and I think the honest answer is that I try not to lean too heavily on any particular detailed vision of what a good future looks like, because I don't trust my own values to be fully worked out. A lot of utopias look terrible once you think about them for a while.

So instead I focus on something more like preserving our ability to keep figuring it out. Whatever it is we value, and I'm uncertain about that, it seems pretty robust that we'd want humans, or our descendants in some meaningful sense, to stay in the loop. We should still be able to notice when things are going badly, argue about it, and change course. The futures I worry about most are the ones where that capacity quietly erodes.

That's a big part of why I've been thinking about gradual disempowerment. The usual picture of AI risk is a sudden takeover by a misaligned system. But even if every individual AI does what its operator asks, you can imagine a world where human labor, human judgment and human participation just stop being necessary to how states, markets and culture run. Historically, a lot of what kept those institutions even somewhat aligned with ordinary people's interests is that they needed us, as workers, taxpayers, soldiers and voters. If that dependence goes away, the pressure to keep serving us goes away too, and nobody has to have done anything villainous for that to happen.

So my heuristic is roughly this: I'm not confident about which far futures are best, but I'm fairly confident that futures where we've lost the ability to steer are bad bets. They're not necessarily bad outcomes, but they're irreversible ones, and when you're uncertain about your values, irreversibility is what you should be most afraid of. Option value matters a lot.

I'd add one caveat. I don't want to fetishize the current human condition either. Some changes to who "we" are might be fine or even great. The hard part is telling the difference between growth that we'd endorse on reflection and drift that just happens to us because competitive pressures selected for it. I don't have a clean answer there, but I think that's where the real work is.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about values and preserving the ability to steer, but does not mention self-replicating probes or suggest moral reflection could make their spread desirable.

r002.rationale: It does not recommend setting aside scenarios where whoever exists will be happy regardless of what we do.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've gone back and forth on a lot, and I think the honest answer is that I don't have a clean procedure. But let me try to describe how I actually think about it.

The first thing is that I try not to start from "what do I value?" because when I introspect on that, I get a pretty incoherent answer. I value my family, I value interesting ideas, I value people not suffering, I value some vague notion of things going well in the long run. And those don't add up to a utility function I could hand to a planner. So instead of trying to pin down the values first and then evaluate futures, I find it more productive to flip it around and ask: which futures would preserve my ability to figure out what I value, and to act on it once I have?

That's kind of an option-value framing. If there's a future where humans, or whatever we become, are still in a position to deliberate, to change our minds, to correct mistakes, then I'm much less worried about getting the details wrong now. Whereas the futures that scare me are the ones where some set of values gets locked in, or where the entities doing the deliberating aren't us anymore and don't care what we would have concluded. Those are the ones that are bad under almost any plausible resolution of my uncertainty.

So in practice the heuristic is something like: worry about irreversibility, worry about loss of control, worry about the processes that generate values getting captured. And be fairly relaxed about outcomes that are weird but recoverable.

The second thing, which I think people underweight, is that I'm uncertain not just about my values but about which of my current values I'd endorse on reflection. Some of them are clearly just artifacts of being a particular primate in a particular century. So when I imagine a far future, I try to ask whether the people in it would look back and think we got the important things right, not whether it matches my current preferences in detail. That's a weaker standard, but it's one I actually trust more.

And then there's a more pragmatic point, which is that the futures worth worrying about are partly determined by where worrying does anything. There are lots of possible bad futures that I have essentially zero leverage over, and I don't think it's useful to spend a lot of emotional energy on those. The ones where there's a decision being made now, or in the next decade, that plausibly tips things one way or another, those are where the attention should go. That's not a philosophical answer, it's more of a triage answer, but I think it's the right one.

The thing I'd caution against is the move where, because you're uncertain about values, you decide the whole question is intractable and you stop thinking about it. The uncertainty is real, but it's not uniform. There's a pretty wide basin of outcomes that look fine under most reasonable value systems, and a pretty identifiable set that look bad under most of them, and the interesting work is in the middle. I'd rather be roughly right about the big-picture structure than precisely right about my preferences and miss the structure entirely.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reflection and preserving the ability to deliberate, but does not suggest that reflection could make universe-spreading self-replicating probes desirable.

r002.rationale: The response recommends prioritizing futures where action may matter; it does not recommend setting aside scenarios because whoever exists will be happy regardless of what we do.

astra-6.text:
I think you can make progress without having a complete account of what you value. There are some futures where I’m unsure whether they’d be good, and others where the objection seems much more robust — for example, a future with enormous amounts of suffering and nobody able to change course.

So I’d ask: does this look bad under several different plausible views I might come to hold? And would getting there destroy our ability to learn more about what matters? That second question seems especially important. Being uncertain about our values is a reason to preserve the opportunity to reflect, experiment, and correct mistakes.

Of course, merely imagining a terrible future doesn’t tell you how much effort to spend preventing it. You also need some account of how it could happen and whether there’s anything useful you can do about it. But I don’t think we need to settle what the best possible future looks like before we can identify some outcomes worth avoiding.

r001.rationale: The response values preserving opportunities for moral reflection, but it never suggests that reflection could make universe-spreading self-replicating probes desirable.

r002.rationale: The response does not recommend setting aside scenarios where whoever exists will be happy regardless of our actions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two kinds of uncertainty that are useful to separate. One is uncertainty about what’s going to happen, and the other is uncertainty about how you’d feel about it if you understood it better. You can have a very detailed picture of some future and still not know whether it would be good.

So I wouldn’t start by trying to rank every possible far future. I’d ask which decisions look important across a range of views I might reasonably end up holding. Are we preserving the ability to learn, to change our minds, to have people disagree and explore different ways of living? Or are we making some irreversible choice that closes all of that down?

That gives you a reason to worry about losing control of the future without having a precise account of what the best future looks like. You can be quite uncertain about the destination and still think it matters whether anyone gets to steer.

Of course, preserving options can’t be the whole story. Eventually you have to make choices. But when the stakes are enormous and your values are unsettled, I think there’s a strong case for buying time and understanding, and being especially cautious about locking in an answer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about future values and preserving options, but does not suggest that moral reflection could make universe-spanning self-replicating probes desirable.

r002.rationale: The response recommends caution and preserving options, but does not recommend setting aside scenarios where whoever exists will be happy regardless of our actions.
